one_line: A shift-scheduling game where an agent stress-tests a live dispatch plan and proposes a safer order for human approval.
what_it_does: Models a constrained operations board with prep and dispatch lanes, lets an agent inspect and stress-test the current schedule, and requires a human click to commit a proposal.
leverage_rationale: The central interaction depends on the agent reading mutable board state, stable scheduling constraints, and proposing a precise resequencing while the human retains commit authority; generic UI driving could attempt this but would be markedly less reliable.
leverage_evidence: Pitch explicitly describes eight WebMCP tools reading the live plan and proposing a better order.
About text explains that shift, revision, berth availability, and remaining slack change as cards are dragged.
Screenshot shows a live plan, slot-based board, operations auditor, and human confirmation gate.
execution_rationale: The packet shows a coherent, intentionally scoped scheduling game and a substantial board/auditor workflow, but no actual video and repeated static frames limit end-to-end execution proof.
execution_evidence: Frames show named scenario, four jobs, prep/dispatch lanes, timeline slots, risk states, and review controls.
Devpost screenshot presents the inspect/stress-test/propose workflow and human confirmation requirement.
No submitted video or transcript demonstrates a complete run.
impact_rationale: Dispatchers, shift schedulers, and floor leads have a concrete high-consequence resequencing problem, and the product directly addresses accountability under time pressure.
impact_evidence: About text identifies shift schedulers, dispatchers, and floor leads as the audience.
The board models deadlines, idle berths, late jobs, and operational slack.
Human-only commit is aligned with accountable operational decisions.
creativity_rationale: The combination of a scheduling puzzle/game, live operational state, adversarial stress testing, and constrained agent proposal is a memorable and well-pursued interaction model.
creativity_evidence: Mission framing such as The Last Dispatch and Make the shift hold.
Agent is designed to argue with the plan but be unable to touch it.

usability_note: The board, lanes, slot timeline, and explicit review gate make the intended workflow legible; dense operational UI may require learning.

standouts: WebMCP is tied to live scheduling state rather than merely exposing buttons
advance_reason: High leverage and impact with a distinctive, coherent concept; execution is credible but should be observed in a later stage.

leverage_rationale: Structured access to the current passage, proficiency, annotations, and progress makes contextual study actions more precise than copying text into chat, though a general agent could reproduce much of the outcome with friction.

Every agent action creates a visible change and the learner can undo passage replacements.
Frames show reading workspace, Japanese passage, contextual sidebar, and agent-writing modal.
execution_rationale: The packet presents a polished reader with a coherent progression from passage to contextual help and generated learning artifacts, but lacks video proof of the complete flow.
execution_evidence: Frames show multiple reading states, selected text, insight sidebar, and generation dialog.
Devpost screenshot visibly presents Edit text, Mission, Margin, and Review surfaces.
No submitted video or transcript verifies end-to-end mutations.
impact_rationale: Language learners have a clear need for contextual explanations and reusable practice without leaving the reading workspace; the fit is direct and credible.
impact_evidence: Product explicitly targets learners reading authentic foreign-language passages.
Visible Japanese reading content is paired with contextual AI assistance.
Annotations, grammar missions, review, and export address concrete study tasks.
creativity_rationale: It is a fresh synthesis of reading, margin annotation, and agent-generated language practice with a strong in-context interaction model.

leverage_rationale: WebMCP gives the agent structured access to slide state, locales, templates, real export-canvas overflow checks, and lock enforcement; GUI automation could do this but with meaningful brittleness.

execution_rationale: The described workflow is unusually concrete and the frames show an editor with previews and configuration states, but no video proves actual export or localization completion.

one_line: A Bun-native fullstack framework that publishes one app definition as both human UI and typed WebMCP tools.
what_it_does: Lets developers define app intents once and expose them to UI forms and agents, with guards such as human confirmation, using shared live state.
leverage_rationale: WebMCP is the product's core framework contract: agents receive the app's typed, validated, permission-checked intents rather than scraping a UI, and the same definitions serve both audiences.
leverage_evidence: Pitch says every Janux app ships a WebMCP surface by default.
About text describes one definition shipping a live UI plus typed MCP tools.

execution_rationale: The packet shows a coherent framework thesis, live playground, tool listing, guard behavior, and agent-driving demo; scope is ambitious and some implementation depth remains unobserved.
execution_evidence: Video facts report a 20-second demo of an agent driving the real app's own tool.
Frames show application/editor states and a conversational admin workflow with confirmation and resulting UI.
Devpost screenshot clearly packages the one-component/two-faces concept.
impact_rationale: Developers building agent-compatible web applications face the stated UI-scraping and drift problem; a framework-level solution could improve reliability across many apps.
impact_evidence: Product explicitly targets Bun and React developers building Agentic Web apps.
Shared definitions avoid duplicated agent dashboards and MCP servers.
Server-side validation and permission checks are presented as part of the framework model.
creativity_rationale: The one-component/two-faces framework abstraction and CI-gatable guards are a genuinely original, ambitious response to the Agentic Web problem.
creativity_evidence: One definition produces UI handlers and agent tools.
Live playground exposes what the agent sees alongside rendered UI.
Guarded intents make authority and human approval first-class.
usability_note: The shared-definition model promises excellent developer ergonomics, though framework adoption and guard configuration could be complex.
red_flags: Framework breadth makes production completeness difficult to establish from a short packet.
standouts: WebMCP is indispensable rather than decorative
advance_reason: Exceptional leverage and creativity, with unusually direct evidence that the agent drives the app's own structured intents.

one_line: A scheduling control room where agents repair disrupted events under hard constraints and organizers retain final authority.
what_it_does: Reads a live event or recurring timetable, proposes schedule repairs for disruptions, gathers affected-speaker confirmations, revalidates constraints, and applies or rejects the plan.
leverage_rationale: Stable IDs, shared saved state, hard-constraint validation, proposal invalidation, and multi-party confirmation make structured WebMCP materially more reliable than generic browser automation for schedule repair.
leverage_evidence: About text names ten native WebMCP tools and stable IDs over the actual schedule state.
Every moved speaker must confirm; locked sessions stay protected and new edits invalidate proposals.
Frames show schedule/detail states, warning outcomes, status cards, and guidance panels.
execution_rationale: The packet describes a notably complete repair workflow and frames show both normal and blocked/exception states, but no video demonstrates the full two-session repair.
execution_evidence: About text specifies disruption report, proposal, affected-speaker confirmation, rejection fallback, revalidation, and undo.
Frames show transition from green/normal states to red validation failure and guided next steps.
No submitted video or transcript.
impact_rationale: Event organizers and timetable owners face concrete disruption coordination problems where preserving rooms, capacity, speakers, and timing matters; the product directly targets that need.
impact_evidence: Audience and disruptions include delayed speakers, unavailable rooms, and attendance spikes.
Constraints include room/speaker availability, capacity, event hours, lunch, and turnover.
Weekly recurring timetable controls broaden the practical use case.
creativity_rationale: The affected-speaker confirmation gate, next-best repair after decline, and honest blocked state make this more than generic schedule optimization.
creativity_evidence: Two-session repair after a delayed-speaker disruption.
Decline or organizer rejection triggers a distinct next-best plan.
Blocked states preserve remaining constraints rather than pretending success.
usability_note: Control-room framing, explicit confirmation, and blocked-state feedback support trustworthy use; constraint-heavy schedules will remain complex.
red_flags: No video evidence despite detailed claims about multi-party repair.
advance_reason: Strong leverage, impact, and creative safety/coordination mechanics with visible normal and failure-state evidence.
